title: Default-Deny Ingress Gate
description: A default-deny ingress gate blocks every inbound packet unless an explicit allow rule matches. It is the foundation of firewall policy: the deny-all rule sits last in the chain, so forgotten or misconfigured services stay invisible instead of accidentally exposed to the internet.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Web Tier Allow 80/443
description: Allows inbound TCP traffic on ports 80 and 443 to reach the web tier while everything else stays blocked. HTTP is kept only for redirecting to HTTPS; the rule is scoped to the load balancer addresses so direct-to-server bypass attempts fail closed.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: SSH Bastion Restriction
description: Restricts SSH port 22 to a single bastion host address, so administrators must hop through one hardened entry point. Direct SSH to any other server from the outside is denied and logged, which shrinks the brute-force attack surface to a single monitored door.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Database Tier Isolation
description: Database servers accept connections only from the application tier subnet, never from the public internet or the web tier directly. This segmentation means a compromised web server still cannot reach the database unless the attacker also pivots into the app tier.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Egress Allowlist for Updates
description: Outbound traffic is denied except to approved software-update mirrors and package registries. Servers can still patch themselves on schedule, but malware on a compromised host cannot phone home or exfiltrate data to arbitrary destinations.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Stateful Return-Traffic Acceptance
description: Accepts inbound packets that belong to an already-established outbound connection, tracked in the firewall's state table. This lets servers receive replies to their own requests without opening any inbound ports, which is how safe browsing and API calls work behind a strict firewall.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: ICMP Rate Limit
description: Limits ICMP echo requests to a small number per second per source, which stops ping floods while keeping legitimate diagnostics working. Bursts above the limit are dropped silently so the firewall does not waste effort answering an attack.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: DNS Egress Pinning
description: Forces all DNS queries to go through the organization's own resolvers by blocking outbound port 53 to anywhere else. This stops malware from using rogue DNS servers for tunneling and lets the security team see and filter every name lookup.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Port-Scan Detection and Drop
description: Watches for the signature of a port scan - many connection attempts to different ports from one source in a short window - and drops the scanner's packets for a cooldown period. Every detection is logged with the source address and the ports probed for later investigation.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Geo-Block High-Risk Regions
description: Blocks inbound traffic from CIDR ranges in regions the business never serves, cutting out a large share of opportunistic attacks. The block lists are refreshed daily from a maintained feed, and legitimate travelers can request temporary exceptions through the help desk.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: QUIC and UDP 443 Allowance
description: Permits UDP port 443 so the QUIC transport used by modern web traffic can function. Without this allowance, browsers fall back to slower TCP connections or fail on networks that only permit the new protocol, so the rule is scoped to known-good destinations.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Management VLAN Segregation
description: Management interfaces for switches, servers, and appliances accept connections only from the dedicated admin VLAN. Even valid credentials fail when presented from any other network, which keeps management planes unreachable from user and guest segments.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: SYN Flood Cookie Protection
description: When the SYN queue fills under flood, the firewall switches to SYN cookies: it encodes connection state into the sequence number instead of storing it. Legitimate clients complete the handshake transparently while spoofed SYNs, which never answer, consume no memory.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Application-Layer HTTP Filtering
description: Inspects HTTP requests past the headers and blocks known-malicious user agents, exploit paths, and oversized payloads. It runs after TLS termination at the edge, so it sees plaintext requests and can stop web attacks that a port-level firewall would wave through.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Log and Alert on Deny
description: Every denied packet is logged with timestamp, source, destination, ports, and the rule that denied it, and high-severity denies trigger immediate alerts. These logs are the raw material for incident response: without them, blocked attacks are invisible and tuning the policy is guesswork.
provenance: Public technical knowledge compiled from standard references and documentation; verified 2026-10-21.
